title: A Topological Spin on Racetrack Memory
abstract: Magnetic racetrack memory requires localized carriers that combine rapid motion, resistance to perturbations and a detectable signal. Here we show how a 360° domain wall in a hollow ferromagnetic tube combines these properties within a single continuous magnetic shell. Two successive magnetization reversals form a bound object whose surrounding domains point in the same direction. Analytical energetics and micromagnetic simulations establish its finite separation, recovery from tested perturbations and current driven transport without microscopic Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction or a maintaining field. The texture's winding resists unwinding while radial rotation carries an energy cost, providing a specific control over stability. Relative rotation of the constituent spins accounts quantitatively for additional displacement during current onset. The wall supports motion at hundreds of metres per second, with transient velocities approaching one kilometre per second at stronger drive. A prepared seven-bit pattern retains its carriers and local readout contrast after pulsed transport and recovery. Curved-track and differential-current tests identify radial stiffness and drive uniformity as controls for intact motion. These results establish a physical basis for fast, locally distinguishable tubular magnetic bits and identify a continuous switching pathway that can be targeted by tailored excitation.
summary: This work proposes a novel magnetic memory bit based on a topologically stabilized $360^\circ$ domain wall confined in a hollow tube. Using micromagnetic simulations, the authors demonstrate that the wall maintains stability and supports ultra-fast, controllable motion without relying on external fields or chiral interactions. This establishes a physical pathway for high-density, fast magnetic data storage.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for a magnetic memory carrier that combines rapid motion, robustness against perturbations, and a clear readout signal, overcoming limitations of existing domain wall and skyrmion concepts.
main_result: A $360^\circ$ domain wall confined in a hollow ferromagnetic tube was shown to be stable, support high-speed motion (up to $1 	ext{ km/s}$ transiently), and retain stored information patterns.
method: The study employs analytical energetics and micromagnetic simulations solving the Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert equation with spin-transfer torque.
model_or_system: The physical system is a $360^\circ$ domain wall within a hollow ferromagnetic tube. The model uses the LLG equation with STT, incorporating topological winding ($W$) as a stabilizing feature, and explicitly excludes external fields or Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction.
key_observables: Winding number ($W$), topological charge ($Q$), carrier velocity (up to $1 	ext{ km/s}$), and retained information patterns (seven-bit pattern).
important_parameters: Current density ($J_s$), exchange stiffness ($A$), and the energy cost associated with radial spin rotation.
main_assumptions: The analysis omits thermal noise and assumes fixed material parameters; stability is governed by geometric and topological constraints rather than external fields.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the magnetic texture of the $360^\circ$ DW, the dependence of energy on separation, and the quantitative contribution of relative spin rotation to the total displacement during current-driven transport.
paper_structure: The paper develops by first establishing the topological nature of the $360^\circ$ DW, then analyzing its dynamics using the LLG equation with STT to quantify the role of internal spin rotation, and finally demonstrating pattern retention under pulsed transport.
why_interesting: While focused on spintronics, the detailed modeling of emergent topological stability and controlled dynamics using continuum equations (LLG) shares mathematical formalism with the study of non-equilibrium dynamics in quantum many-body systems.
